ideas.title: 24/7 named-filer retainer for CRA reporting
ideas.one_liner: A follow-the-sun 'fractional PSIRT' that pre-registers, drills and files CRA Article 14 vulnerability reports on the ENISA portal for small connected-device makers.
ideas.customer: EU and non-EU manufacturers of connected products with roughly 5-250 staff and no 24/7 security team. Examples are smart-home, IP camera, e-bike and e-scooter electronics, EV charger, industrial IoT gateway, 3D printer and consumer robotics makers. Their CEO or head of product pays.
ideas.problem: Since 11 Sept 2026, manufacturers must send an early warning within 24 hours of becoming aware of an actively exploited vulnerability, a fuller notice within 72 hours, and a final report later. This covers products already on the market, including 2019 models. Fines reach EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover. The ENISA portal has no API at launch and needs 39 manual fields. Filers must be named individuals with EU Login and MFA. Picking the wrong coordinator CSIRT can invalidate a filing. The platform's 72-hour counter can show a compliant filing as overdue. Emailing a national CSIRT does not count. Small makers have no one awake on a Sunday who knows any of this.
ideas.solution: Sell a monthly retainer with four parts. (1) A pre-flight setup: named EU Login accounts, a documented coordinator-CSIRT choice, a product-to-Member-State map and the required vulnerability contact. (2) A one-page intake form and an 'awareness decision log' that keeps independent 24h/72h/14-day clocks and a defensible record of when the manufacturer became aware. (3) A rotating on-call engineer, holding one of the up-to-20 secondary filer seats under the manufacturer's written designation, who drafts and pastes the 39-field early warning within hours. (4) Twice-yearly tabletop drills that produce an audit-ready evidence file. The manufacturer stays legally responsible. We supply speed and process, not scanners.
ideas.why_now: Article 14 became binding on 11 Sept 2026 and the single reporting platform went live the same day. Registration guidance only started rolling out on 31 July. No CRA harmonised standard was in the Official Journal as of late August, and notified-body capacity is a 'best-efforts' December 2026 target. Small makers therefore have no standards shortcut and must run the reporting process by hand.
ideas.revenue_model: Setup fee of EUR 1,000-1,500. Retainer of EUR 250-600 per month by product count. Incident filing package of EUR 2-4k per event. Drill add-on of EUR 800. Later, referral or bundle deals with cyber insurers, notified-body consultants and contract manufacturers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is a named human with a valid account, awake at 3am, making the 'awareness' judgment call. Scanner vendors are everywhere, but nobody sells the person and the drill. Evidence: the ENISA portal guide says 'Automate the preparation, not the filing' and lists no API, 39 fields, named-person accounts, the wrong-CSIRT risk and the misaligned 72h counter (https://craevidence.com/cra-compliance/enisa-srp-onboarding). An ENISA survey found 20% of SMEs were unsure the CRA even applied to them (https://www.techtarget.com/cybersecurity/feature/EU-Cyber-Resilience-Act-reporting-What-CISOs-need-to-know). Greenbone's readiness review found the platform still in testing two weeks before go-live and no standards published (https://www.greenbone.net/en/blog/cra-article-14-readiness-status/). ENISA launch note: https://www.enisa.europa.eu/news/the-cra-single-reporting-platform-is-launched.
ideas.first_30_days: Turn the public ENISA and Commission material into a free 'SRP pre-flight' checklist and a 24h/72h clock template, and publish both. Recruit 4-6 freelance product-security engineers across EU, US and Asia time zones for a rotation. Cold-message about 300 product-security, CE-compliance and CTO contacts at hardware makers (RED and CE registries, hardware crowdfunding lists). Offer 5 founding pilots at EUR 99 per month plus a free first drill. Book a tabletop drill with each pilot and convert the drill output into the case study.

ideas.title: EUDR reference-number desk for downstream buyers
ideas.one_liner: An inbox-and-validator service that collects, checks and vaults EUDR reference numbers and plot GeoJSON from suppliers, sold to downstream operators and via customs brokers.
ideas.customer: Mid-size EU importers, traders and manufacturers who buy EUDR goods (wood and furniture components, coffee, cocoa, leather, rubber parts, palm derivatives) after a first operator has placed them on the market. The second channel is customs brokers and freight forwarders who white-label the desk.
ideas.problem: From 30 Dec 2026, large and medium operators and traders must comply. Downstream operators no longer file due diligence statements but must collect and keep upstream reference and verification numbers for 5 years. They cannot place goods on the market if the numbers are missing when evidently required. One guide estimates 15-30 minutes per supplier per plot for chasing, format fixes and plausibility checks, which is 'several person-weeks' at 150 suppliers, every year. Typical data faults are self-intersecting polygons from phone apps, areas off by 100x, national coordinate systems instead of WGS 84, plots outside the declared country and duplicates.
ideas.solution: A forward-to inbox and portal that (1) extracts reference and verification numbers and GeoJSON from supplier emails, PDFs, spreadsheets and invoices; (2) runs geometry checks on closed rings, self-intersection, WGS 84 with six decimals, the 4-hectare polygon rule, plot inside the declared country, duplicates and area versus tonnage plausibility; (3) auto-sends the supplier a plain-language fix request in their language, with a mobile-friendly plot-drawing link; (4) keeps a 5-year evidence vault; and (5) shows a per-purchase-order 'safe to ship or resell' status. Ship a free public GeoJSON validator first as the lead magnet.
ideas.why_now: The 30 Dec 2026 application date is fixed. The Commission's May 2026 review said the regulation will not be reopened and proposed a wider product scope through a draft delegated act, so more mid-size buyers will be pulled in. The EU TRACES NT system was reported not fully operational for the December 2025 date, so integration surprises remain.
ideas.revenue_model: SaaS tiers of EUR 79-249 per month by supplier count, plus EUR 1-3 per consignment checked. White-label to brokers at EUR 0.50-3 per declaration or a flat EUR 500-2,000 per month. Optional paid supplier-data cleanup projects.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Filing software is crowded, but 'no DDS needed' makes downstream buyers feel safe while they inherit the messiest job: chasing numbers by email from dozens of suppliers, with a 5-year retention duty and a day-one commercial gate. As one guide puts it, 'Market access, not the fine, is the mechanism that will change behaviour first', because customers cannot resell goods without the numbers (https://www.omnia-analytics.at/en/blog/eudr-2026-operator-data-requirements, which also gives the 15-30 minute estimate and the polygon error list). Incorrect polygon format is reported as a leading cause of DDS rejection (https://www.coolset.com/academy/eudr-geolocation-requirements-how-to-collect-and-validate-gps-polygon-data-for-your-dds). Manufacturers 'do not consider themselves agricultural commodity buyers' yet inherit the duty (https://www.regilient.ai/blog/eudr-due-diligence-product-traceability-compliance). Fixing data at the supplier gives free viral distribution, because each supplier serves many buyers.
ideas.first_30_days: Build the public GeoJSON checker using open geometry libraries and rank it for searches like 'EUDR GeoJSON self-intersection error'. Pitch 3 customs brokers and 3 coffee, timber or furniture importers with a manual concierge version: they forward supplier emails and you return a cleaned register within 48 hours. Charge EUR 500 for a one-off audit of their existing supplier files. Use the audits to find the 10 most common data faults and build fix templates.

ideas.title: Supplier-side questionnaire firewall citing the VSME cap
ideas.one_liner: A forward-to tool that answers big customers' ESG, NIS2 and EUDR questionnaires from one evidence vault and flags which questions the law says a small supplier can decline.
ideas.customer: EU SMEs and small mid-caps (under 1,000 staff) that supply larger companies, bought through accountants, tax advisors and chambers of commerce who add it as a service to their clients.
ideas.problem: Since Omnibus I took effect on 18 March 2026, CSRD-scope buyers cannot require value-chain partners with 1,000 or fewer employees to provide more sustainability information than the voluntary SME standard (VSME) sets out. The VSME basic module covers business description, workforce, energy and Scope 1 and 2 emissions. The cap does not cover NIS2 security questionnaires, EUDR data, voluntary customer targets or bid competition. Suppliers still get differently formatted questionnaires from every customer and lender, and most cannot tell which asks are legally capped.
ideas.solution: Suppliers forward each customer questionnaire (Excel, PDF or portal export) to an inbox. The tool parses it and maps each question to a canonical evidence vault: VSME basic answers, energy and payroll-derived Scope 1 and 2 numbers, a NIS2-lite control evidence set, and a supplier code of conduct. It auto-drafts answers. It also classifies every question as 'inside the cap', 'outside the cap, with a cited polite decline paragraph', or 'not covered by the cap (NIS2, EUDR, voluntary)'. The vault is built by pulling data the accountant already holds. Accountants get a multi-client dashboard.
ideas.why_now: The cap is 6 months old and the VSME Delegated Act was published in July 2026, so customers' procurement teams are still sending old-format questionnaires. Germany's NIS2 law took effect on 6 Dec 2025 and BSI says regulated entities will grow from about 4,500 to about 29,500, which multiplies supplier security questionnaires. CSDDD also limits information requests to smaller firms, but application is not until 2029.
ideas.revenue_model: White-label to accountancies at EUR 15-30 per client per month, or direct at EUR 49-99 per month per SME. Add EUR 150-300 for a one-off 'initial vault build' for firms not served by an accountant.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The crowded market sells to large buyers who send questionnaires. The legally new wedge is the supplier's right to refuse, plus the accountant, who already holds energy and payroll data and is trusted. Evidence: after 18 March 2026 large CSRD companies 'cannot require value-chain partners with 1,000 or fewer employees to provide more sustainability information than ... VSME', but the same source warns that 'Nothing stops a buyer choosing the bidder who turned up with clean, current numbers' and that Scope 1 and 2 are non-negotiable, so suppliers need both a decline lever and a ready pack (https://www.dashe.ai/blog/big-customer-asked-for-your-emissions/). Suppliers to NIS2 entities 'should expect questionnaires' and sending a 300-question form is common (https://www.3rdrisk.com/blog/seven-nis2-questions-to-ask). Germany's NIS2 registration had only 38.5% compliance by the March 2026 deadline (https://www.cloudmagazin.com/en/2026/03/22/nis2-and-saas-supply-chain-compliance-gap/).
ideas.first_30_days: Collect 30 real questionnaires by offering accountants a free 'questionnaire triage' in exchange for the redacted files. Hand-map them to a 60-row canonical answer sheet. Build the classify-and-decline prototype on that set. Pitch 5 small accounting firms and 2 chamber-of-commerce sustainability desks with a live demo on a client's own questionnaire. Aim for 3 paying accountancy pilots.

ideas.title: Test-once PFAS proof registry for packaging importers
ideas.one_liner: A SKU-level registry and group-buy of accredited PFAS lab reports, so importers of the same factory's food packaging share one test and can produce an authority-ready dossier fast.
ideas.customer: EU importers, wholesalers and white-label brands of grease-resistant paper and fibre food packaging (takeaway boxes, bakery bags, burger wraps, pizza boxes, cups), plus online B2B packaging shops. Owners, purchasing or QA managers pay.
ideas.problem: Since 12 Aug 2026 the packaging regulation bans PFAS in food-contact packaging above limits (25 ppb per non-polymeric substance, 250 ppb sum, 50 ppm total PFAS), with no grandfathering for stock made earlier. Compliance guides say supplier self-declarations are not proof and that importers and producers carry the liability, with accredited-lab reports needed per packaging type. Authorities can request the technical documentation on short notice. There is no harmonised EU test method and lab capacity is finite. Each importer paying separately for the same factory's product is wasteful.
ideas.solution: A registry keyed to product specification, coating, factory and production lot. Factories, labs and importers upload accredited lab reports (cheap total organic fluorine screening first, then targeted LC-MS/MS). Other importers of the same factory and spec can match and attach the report to their own technical file. A lot-matching check and re-test reminders keep the proof valid, and an 'authority request pack' export assembles the file in one click. Group-buy: when several importers sell the same SKU, the platform pools the cost of one accredited test and negotiates volume prices with 2-3 labs. Each importer remains legally responsible, so the tool shows exactly what evidence it does and does not cover.
ideas.why_now: The ban applied on 12 Aug 2026, six weeks ago, and stock made before then cannot be sold. Labs expect demand to climb through enforcement and there is no harmonised method yet, so evidence quality varies.
ideas.revenue_model: EUR 150-400 per verified report access, EUR 25 per month per SKU for monitoring and re-test alerts, plus a 10-15% margin on group-purchased lab tests. Optional paid dossier assembly at EUR 300-600.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Every importer treats PFAS proof as its own cost, but the object being proven is the packaging type. The same few hundred factory SKUs flow through thousands of importers, which creates network effects for a 'test once, verify per lot' registry that no consultancy or lab has an incentive to build. Evidence: guides state that 'self-declarations from suppliers do not constitute proof' and that certificates of analysis are needed per packaging type (https://www.certivo.com/blog-details/ppwr-pfas-ban-in-food-contact-packaging-what-manufacturers-must-have-ready-by-august-2026); the ban has no grandfather clause and responsibility falls on manufacturers and importers (https://www.kivo.nl/en/knowledge-base/pfas-ban-in-food-packaging-what-does-it-mean-for-your-products/); testing runs from a few hundred euros for screening to several thousand for targeted analysis, labs have limited capacity, and no harmonised EU method exists (https://pakfactory.com/blog/how-to-test-packaging-for-pfas; https://foodpackagingforum.org/news/ppwr-pfas-limits-apply-from-august-12).
ideas.first_30_days: Sign volume pricing with 2 accredited labs for TOF screening and targeted panels. Recruit 10 importers from packaging trade associations, LinkedIn groups and B2B packaging marketplaces. Ask them to list their top 20 SKUs and factories, then find overlaps between them. Run the first pooled test for the most-shared SKU at a per-importer cost far below a solo test. Publish a free 'PFAS status per SKU' lookup to attract more importers. Legal-review the shared-report disclaimer language with a food-contact lawyer.

ideas.title: Battery passport starter that feeds on repair-shop events
ideas.one_liner: A cheap battery-passport package for e-bike and small pack makers, plus a repair-shop scanning app that supplies the lifecycle events the passport is legally supposed to track.
ideas.customer: Small and mid-size European e-bike, e-scooter and cargo-bike brands, pack assemblers, and industrial or storage battery integrators above 2 kWh. The battery passport must exist from 18 Feb 2027. Independent repair shops and refurbishers are the second user group.
ideas.problem: From 18 Feb 2027, LMT, EV and industrial batteries over 2 kWh need a passport reachable by QR code and linked to a unique identifier. The Annex XIII list has 71 entries, but 'not every field is due in February 2027': fields are day-one, modelled-now-populated-later, or waiting on secondary legislation. Access-rights rules are slipping to Q4 2026 and key standards are still in draft. Passports must track state of health, cycle counts and status changes after repurposing or remanufacturing. As one guide says, 'a once-published PDF or marketing microsite is not enough'. Enterprise passport platforms are priced for large firms with compliance teams.
ideas.solution: Two products. (1) A brand starter package: a field-status mapper that says which of the 71 fields are due now, later or pending; ISO/IEC 15459-style unique ID and QR generation; a hosted passport page; and a written-authorisation template so the brand can legally delegate passport management to us. (2) A free repair-shop and refurbisher app that scans the QR, logs state-of-health tests, cell swaps, cycle data and second-life events, and pushes them into the brand's passport. Shops get a free workflow tool and repair leads. Brands pay for the passport and the event stream. This also lines up with the replaceable-battery rule that applies from 18 Feb 2027 and with the Right to Repair Directive.
ideas.why_now: The passport deadline is under 5 months away and the access-rights implementing act is late. Replaceable portable batteries and e-bike batteries become an obligation on the same date. Eighteen Member States had not notified full transposition of the Right to Repair Directive by September 2026, which leaves national repair rules unsettled while shops still have to service batteries.
ideas.revenue_model: Brand setup of EUR 2-5k. Subscription of roughly EUR 1-3 per battery per year (or a EUR 300-1,500 per month floor). Optional per-event fee for verified state-of-health tests. Later, a paid API for insurers and second-life buyers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Everyone sells 'publish a QR page'. The law's real burden is a lifecycle record kept consistent across systems and updated when the battery is serviced or repurposed, and that happens in repair shops that no passport vendor serves. Evidence: 'The hard part is not publishing a page. The hard part is keeping model-level, plant-level, and individual-battery records consistent', passports must track state of health, cycle counts and status changes, and batteries allow the operator to authorise another actor in writing to manage the passport (https://infodpp.eu/en/blog/battery-dpp-deadline-february-2027/). Mid-scale companies are named as the likely pressure point (https://www.batterytechonline.com/design-manufacturing/preparing-for-eu-battery-qr-code-standards-in-2027) and passport software is described as badly priced for small manufacturers (https://dpp-tool.com/en/guide/dpp-software-comparison/). Replaceability and spare-battery availability from 18 Feb 2027 are covered at https://www.intertek.com/blog/2025/06-27-2027-reqs-for-removability-and-replaceability-of-batteries-in-electrical-products/. Right to Repair transposition gap: https://www.eunews.it/en/2026/09/25/right-to-repair-italy-and-17-other-countries-have-failed-to-transpose-the-directive-eu-infringement-proceedings-begin/.
ideas.first_30_days: Build a spreadsheet-based field-status mapper for the 71 fields and offer it as a free download. Contact 30 small e-bike brands and pack assemblers found through European trade fairs, cycling industry associations and importer lists. Sell 3 paid 'passport readiness sprint' engagements at EUR 1.5-3k each that end with a hosted pilot passport for one battery model. In parallel, recruit 10 independent e-bike shops to test the scan-and-log app on real service jobs.

ideas.title: Foreign-Ties Clearance Pack for SBIR Startups
ideas.one_liner: A fixed-price, agency-ready foreign-involvement and cyber-readiness dossier priced to fit inside the SBIR technical-assistance allowance, so the startup pays nothing out of pocket.
ideas.customer: SBIR/STTR Phase I and Phase II applicants and awardees (DoD, DOE, NSF, NIH, EPA). Secondary buyers are seed and VC funds with SBIR-heavy portfolios that need LP-level attestations for their companies.
ideas.problem: The Small Business Innovation and Economic Security Act (S. 3971, signed April 13, 2026, extends SBIR/STTR through FY2031) makes agencies run risk-based due diligence on every applicant. The review covers foreign ownership and financial ties, foreign affiliations of key personnel, licensing deals and joint ventures, and links to the UFLPA, Chinese Military-Industrial Complex, Commerce Entity and Section 889 lists. It also covers cybersecurity practices, patent analysis and employee analysis. Applicants must file disclosures. A 4-person startup has no idea what an agency will find in its cap table (LPs behind the VC funds), co-inventors, or contractors. Agencies may notify of a denial only 'as appropriate', so a rejection may come with no explanation.
ideas.solution: A software-plus-analyst service that ingests the cap table, team list, patents and vendor list. It does look-through on investors (SEC Form ADV and Form D, GLEIF, OpenCorporates). It screens every name against the free BIS Consolidated Screening List and the UFLPA and CMIC lists. It checks co-inventor and employee affiliations (USPTO PatentsView, ORCID) and takes a NIST 800-171/SPRS cyber baseline. Output is a disclosure-ready packet, a red-flag remediation memo (for example 'restructure this side letter'), and a yearly re-screen. Sold as a vendor the awardee can pick for technical and business assistance (T&BA) money.
ideas.why_now: S. 3971 was signed April 13, 2026. The T&BA allowance was raised to $6,500 per Phase I and $50,000 per Phase II, and it now explicitly covers 'cybersecurity assistance' and 'screening for potential foreign involvement'. The lapse from October 2025 to April 2026 created a backlog: DOE alone opened about $147M of FY25 Phase II on July 22, 2026, and the FY26 Genesis Mission Phase I is open. Every awardee now faces the new diligence for the first time.
ideas.revenue_model: $2,500 to $6,500 flat per Phase I (fits under the $6,500 T&BA cap, so it is free to the founder). $15k to $50k per Phase II package. $1,200 per year for a re-screen subscription when the cap table changes. VC portfolio bundles at $500 to $1,000 per company.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Congress created an earmarked wallet for exactly this service, and the buyer has zero price sensitivity because the money can't be spent on anything else. S. 3971 Section 7 amends Section 9(q) to allow T&BA funds for 'cybersecurity assistance' and 'screening for potential foreign involvement', up to $6,500 (Phase I) and $50,000 (Phase II) per project, and lets recipients choose their own vendors. Section 2 (new Section 9(vv)) lists the diligence factors agencies must assess (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-119s3971enr/html/BILLS-119s3971enr.htm). DOE confirms the April 13, 2026 signing, extension through FY2031, new security due-diligence mandates, and the reopened Phase II money (https://www.energy.gov/technologycommercialization/doe-small-business-innovation-research-sbir-and-small-business). The hard part is not screening names but LP-level look-through on venture funds, which is opaque and which no compliance vendor packages for a 4-person startup. Caveat: I could not confirm which agencies have opened T&BA vendor lists yet, so check that first.
ideas.first_30_days: Week 1: build a free 'SBIR foreign-risk self-check' web tool on top of the BIS Consolidated Screening List API and the UFLPA list. Use it as the lead magnet. Weeks 1 to 2: pull the last 12 months of Phase I/II awardees from the public SBIR.gov awards data and email 300 founders quoting the exact statute language. Weeks 2 to 4: manually produce 5 free dossiers for design partners to learn where the LP look-through breaks. Ask each agency SBIR office (start with DOE OTC, NSF and Navy) how to be listed as a T&BA vendor. Close 5 paid packs at $2.5k to $6.5k.

ideas.title: Transition Sponsor Radar for Strategic Breakthrough Awards
ideas.one_liner: A subscription and dossier service that maps each SBIR Phase II technology to the specific budget line, program office and person who could commit to a Program Objective Memorandum (POM), which the new $30M Strategic Breakthrough awards require.
ideas.customer: Phase II awardees in DoD-funded SBIR (thousands per year) that want Phase III or Strategic Breakthrough money, plus SBIR-focused VCs and advisors who decide which portfolio companies to back.
ideas.problem: Strategic Breakthrough awards run up to $30M over 48 months, but a company needs at least one prior Phase II, at least 100% matching funds from new private capital or non-SBIR government money, and, for DoD, a 'commitment for inclusion in a program objective memorandum' from the acquisition executive or higher. Agencies must contract within 90 days of a proposal. The technology is rarely the bottleneck. The bottleneck is finding the one person with authority over a budget line, and knowing the POM calendar, since the POM is written 18 to 24 months ahead of the fiscal year. The public data (R-1/R-2 RDT&E exhibits, P-1 procurement lines, FPDS contracts, SBIR.gov awards) exists but is not indexed by technology.
ideas.solution: Build a searchable graph linking SBIR.gov Phase II abstracts to R-2 program elements, project numbers and named PEOs/PMs, and to FPDS Phase III contracts (where SBIR data-rights clauses appear). For each customer, produce a 'sponsor dossier': the top 5 program elements that could absorb the tech, the POM cycle dates, who to call, precedent Phase III transitions, and candidate match-fund sources. Add a monthly alert when a relevant program element grows or a new Phase III model contract appears.
ideas.why_now: The Strategic Breakthrough allocation (up to 0.50% of an agency's R&D budget where R&D exceeds $100M) takes effect in FY2026 and runs to September 30, 2031. Agencies must also create standardized Phase I/II/III model contracts and track direct-to-Phase-II, strategic breakthrough and Phase III awards in the database. Data on where transitions happen will become far richer as this reporting starts.
ideas.revenue_model: $12k to $20k per tech-specific sponsor dossier, paid partly from the $50k Phase II T&BA allowance. $1,500 per month subscription for alerts and updates. $5k per month for SBIR-focused VC funds screening deals. Success fee on Phase III wins (1% to 3%) as an optional add-on.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is not funding, it is a named budget-holder who will put a line in a POM, and that map is buildable from public documents no one has joined to SBIR data. S. 3971 Section 3 (new Section 9(ff)(3)) sets the $30M cap, 48-month term, one prior Phase II, 100% match, DoD POM-commitment requirement and 90-day contracting deadline. Section 6 requires 'simplified and standardized procedures and model contracts' for Phase III. Section 8 requires the database to track Phase III prime and subcontract awards. All at https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-119s3971enr/html/BILLS-119s3971enr.htm. The award-size thresholds the SBA gave for April 2026 ($323,090 Phase I, $2,153,927 Phase II without SBA approval, https://www.sbir.gov/about) show how small the normal awards are next to a $30M award, so the sponsor commitment becomes the step everyone is scrambling for.
ideas.first_30_days: Download the SBIR.gov awards dataset and the latest DoD RDT&E R-2 exhibits (comptroller.defense.gov). Use an LLM to embed and match 200 recent Phase II abstracts to program elements, then have a former acquisition officer sanity-check the top matches. Give 10 Phase II founders a free one-page 'sponsor map' for their own tech. Convert 3 of them to a $12k dossier. Pitch 2 SBIR-focused VC funds a paid pilot on their portfolio.

ideas.title: Market Rulebook Red Team for New Venues
ideas.one_liner: Turn a trading venue's plain-English rulebook into an executable model, then use adversarial agents to find manipulation exploits and propose rule patches before real attackers do.
ideas.customer: Operators of new or small marketplaces: CFTC-registered event-contract and prediction-market venues, tokenized-asset and crypto exchanges, carbon-credit registries, energy and capacity market operators, GPU-compute spot exchanges, and ad-auction platforms.
ideas.problem: Modern electronic markets are built for speed and transparency, which has 'created new attack surfaces and systemic risks', and they 'can be manipulated in ways unanticipated by their designers'. Venues test their matching engine software, but nobody systematically tests the market rules themselves (settlement sources, auction tie-breaks, position limits, fee rebates) for exploits. Regulators expect venues to show their contracts and rules resist manipulation, but there is no standard way to prove it.
ideas.solution: An agent pipeline. Step 1: an LLM converts the rulebook or tariff PDF into a formal mechanism spec (order types, matching rules, settlement, fees). Step 2: an agent-based simulator with attacker agents searches for profitable manipulation strategies (wash trading, spoofing and layering, oracle or settlement-source attacks, self-dealing through fee rebates, cross-market squeezes). Step 3: it proposes rule patches and re-runs the attacks as regression tests. Deliver a fuzz report and a CI-style re-run whenever the rules change.
ideas.why_now: DARPA's Intrinsic Market Resilience (IMR) program, with a proposers day October 1, 2026, abstracts due October 22 and proposals due December 7, 2026, explicitly bets that LLM automation plus rigorous modeling can automatically model market designs, find weaknesses and recommend repairs. New event-contract, tokenized and compute markets are launching faster than their rulebooks can be reviewed. LLMs only recently became good enough at turning long legal text into formal specs.
ideas.revenue_model: $25k to $60k fixed-price rulebook audit. $3k to $8k per month for continuous re-testing when rules or fee schedules change. Possible subcontract or teaming revenue on DARPA IMR or follow-on federal work.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: A rulebook is code that nobody compiles. DARPA is paying to build the compiler-plus-fuzzer, and the same tool works on any venue, so the government-funded R&D is a free market validation of the product category. The IMR page states the problem ('manipulated in ways unanticipated by their designers'), names markets from 'equities and bonds to energy and cloud computing resources', and describes the LLM-plus-formal-modeling approach: https://www.darpa.mil/research/programs/intrinsic-market-resilience-imr. Caveat: the public page names no specific exploits and says nothing about commercial adoption, so the private-sector demand (for example the CFTC's requirement that contracts not be readily susceptible to manipulation) is my inference from background knowledge, not from the DARPA page.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick 3 public rulebooks or tariffs (a new prediction-market venue, a public energy market tariff, a carbon registry methodology). Run the pipeline and publish 3 short teardown posts showing a concrete exploit and a patch. Email the compliance and product heads of 30 newly launched venues with their own teardown. Sell 2 fixed-price audits at $25k. In parallel, submit an abstract by October 22 or offer teaming to IMR prime bidders.

ideas.title: Through-the-Package Drug Verification Library
ideas.one_liner: A subscription spectral fingerprint library and scan-on-receipt workflow that lets pharmacies and wholesalers verify what is actually in a sealed vial or blister pack, using off-the-shelf handheld Raman/NIR devices.
ideas.customer: 503A/503B compounding pharmacies and telehealth GLP-1 dispensers receiving vials or API from overseas, secondary wholesalers and repackagers, hospital pharmacies, and med-spa distributors.
ideas.problem: ARPA-H states that drug-related morbidity and mortality cost $528 billion per year, that recalls affect the medication of over 150 million Americans each year, that 'most recalls only happen after patients are exposed', and that only a small percentage of imported drugs are sampled and tested at ports, a process that takes weeks. Serialization under DSCSA tracks the box (package-level identifiers, 24-hour notification of illegitimate product), not the molecule inside it, so a convincing counterfeit or diluted vial passes every paperwork check.
ideas.solution: Do not build hardware. Rent or resell existing handheld Raman/NIR units, and build the proprietary part: a reference library of authentic and adulterated finished-dose spectra measured through blisters, vials and prefilled pens, plus a classifier and a chain-of-custody report (photo, lot number, spectrum, pass/fail/uncertain). Uncertain results route to a partner lab for confirmatory HPLC. The library improves with every scan.
ideas.why_now: ARPA-H's FASTPASS program (solicitation ARPA-H-SOL-26-160; solution summaries due September 21, 2026, full proposals November 10, 2026) is funding through-packaging sensing (TA1 SAMPLE) and analytics (TA2 DETECT), which signals that the sensing hardware and spectroscopy science are mature enough to commercialize. GLP-1 volume and compounding have widened the exposure of small dispensers who have no way to check incoming product.
ideas.revenue_model: $1 to $3 per scan (usage SaaS), $300 per month device rental, $150 to $400 per escalated lab confirmation, and $6k to $24k per year library license for wholesalers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: DSCSA verifies labels and traceability, not contents, and ARPA-H itself says the gap is one 'no single agency, manufacturer, or current technology can close alone'. That leaves room for a private data product. The moat is the library of through-package spectra, not the scanner, and it compounds with every customer scan. Evidence: https://arpa-h.gov/explore-funding/programs/fastpass ($528B, 150M Americans, 'only a small percentage of imported drugs are sampled and tested at ports', TA1 SAMPLE and TA2 DETECT) and https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-supply-chain-integrity/drug-supply-chain-security-act-dscsa (package-level identification and 24-hour illegitimate-product notification). Caveat: the ARPA-H page did not give product types or counterfeit prevalence, and the GLP-1 exposure is my inference from public FDA alerts.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick 10 high-volume SKUs (injectable GLP-1 vials and pens plus a few high-value generics). Buy authentic references, make in-house dilution and wrong-API samples with a partner lab, rent two handhelds, and collect spectra through the packaging. Offer 3 compounding pharmacies and 2 regional wholesalers a free 30-day pilot with scan-on-receipt. Convert to paid on a per-scan plan. Skip the FASTPASS proposal unless a university partner handles it.

ideas.title: PFAS Land-Application History Reports for Farmland
ideas.one_liner: A 'Phase I environmental site assessment' for PFAS on farmland, built from biosolids land-application records and upstream discharger data, sold to lenders, farmland funds and appraisers before the sensors exist.
ideas.customer: Farm Credit associations and ag banks, farmland investment funds, rural appraisers and title firms, and farmers or buyers who need to show a field is clean.
ideas.problem: EPA released Draft Guidance for Reducing Risk from PFOA and PFOS in Biosolids on July 1, 2026, noting that sewage sludge may carry PFAS from industrial dischargers, landfills and homes. Yet EPA's own FY2026 SBIR Phase I topics still ask small businesses to invent 'Treatment of PFAS in Wastewater Sewage Sludge and Biosolids' and 'Sensors to Detect PFAS in Environmental Matrices', so cheap field screening does not exist. Lenders and buyers are pricing farmland today with no way to know whether a field received sludge, from which plant, and with what upstream industrial inputs.
ideas.solution: A desktop screening report per parcel. It combines state biosolids land-application permits and site reports (obtained by scraping and automated public-records requests), the treatment plant's upstream industrial dischargers, soil and hydrology data, and a risk tier. Higher tiers trigger a sampling plan run by a partner lab using EPA Method 1633. Deliver in the lender's existing environmental-diligence workflow, and later offer an API.
ideas.why_now: The July 1, 2026 EPA draft guidance turns PFAS in biosolids from a research topic into something lenders must ask about. EPA's Sept 24, 2026 SBIR solicitation ($100k per Phase I, 6 months, closes Nov 8, 2026) is paying for the sensing tools, so cheap field tests are years away and records-based screening is the only option now.
ideas.revenue_model: $400 to $1,200 per desktop parcel report. $2k to $6k with coordinated sampling (margin on lab work). $20k to $60k per year API or portfolio subscriptions for lenders and farmland funds.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The government is paying to invent PFAS sensors that don't exist yet, but the lend/buy/insure decision is being made now on paper records, so the winning product is the record-linkage layer, not the sensor. EPA's FY2026 SBIR Phase I topics list 1B (PFAS in sewage sludge and biosolids) and 2A (PFAS sensors in environmental matrices), $100,000 and 6 months each: https://www.epa.gov/sbir/how-apply-sbir-contract. EPA's biosolids page lists the July 1, 2026 Draft Guidance and states that sludge may carry PFAS from upstream dischargers: https://www.epa.gov/biosolids. Lenders already require site assessments for gas stations and dry cleaners, and a PFAS-on-farmland version is the missing sibling. Caveat: the EPA pages I could fetch gave no land-application tonnage or state-by-state record availability, so records access must be checked before committing to a state.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick 1 or 2 states where biosolids land-application permits are public (verify first). Assemble records for the 20 largest treatment plants and build 25 sample reports on real parcels. Approach 5 Farm Credit associations, 3 farmland funds and 5 rural appraisers with a free report on a parcel they already own or are underwriting. Sign a lab partner for sampling. Close the first 3 paid pilots at $400 to $1,200 per parcel.

ideas.title: SNAP-Ready Kits for Corner Stores
ideas.one_liner: A UPC-level 'variety counter' plus a pre-built wholesale fill kit that tells a convenience store exactly what to stock to keep SNAP authorization under USDA's new staple-food rule.
ideas.customer: Independent convenience stores, bodegas, small groceries and dollar-format stores that accept SNAP (USDA counts 269,217 authorized retailers, with small-format stores hit hardest). The store owner pays for the audit and kit. Secondary payers are the local cash-and-carry wholesalers and jobbers who earn incremental case sales, and city or state health departments that fund healthy-corner-store programs.
ideas.problem: USDA's final rule (effective July 7, 2026; implementation Nov 4, 2026) raises the stocking floor from 3 to 7 varieties in each of 4 staple categories (28 varieties), with 3 stocking units each (84 units) and perishables in 3 categories. The counting rules are counterintuitive: brown and white rice are one variety, all bread is one variety, and brands and flavors do not count. USDA's own analysis of 121,294 small-format stores found only 52% already stock enough dairy varieties and 63% enough protein, which implies roughly 58,000 stores short on dairy alone. Stores are assessed at reauthorization (every 5 years, about 54,000 stores a year) or at any time. Owners have no tool that tells them what to buy, and commenters said the rule is infeasible for small stores.
ideas.solution: An SMS and web tool. The owner uploads a POS export or photographs shelves. A classifier maps UPCs to USDA's variety groups, using the rule's Group 1 and Group 2 counting logic, and returns a gap list such as 'need 3 more dairy varieties and 2 more protein varieties, buy these SKUs'. A sold-through kit pre-negotiated with a local wholesaler uses the lowest-spoilage items that fit small refrigeration. The tool also produces a USDA evidence pack (dated photos, invoices, variety ledger) for reauthorization or a compliance review. A 'keep or drop SNAP' ROI calculator is built in, because most small stores earn little from SNAP.
ideas.why_now: USDA published the final rule on May 8, 2026 and the enforcement-ready implementation date is Nov 4, 2026, about five weeks out. The prior interim standard was only 3 varieties per category, so almost every small store has a gap to close. USDA also says it can assess any retailer at any time, and every store hits reauthorization within 5 years, so demand arrives as a rolling wave rather than a single date.
ideas.revenue_model: $79 one-time shelf audit, or free through wholesaler partners. Kit sold at wholesale plus a 10-15% margin, or a referral fee from the wholesaler. $29 per month monitoring with auto-reorder and evidence-pack refresh. Grant-funded 100-store packages ($500-1,500 per store) sold to health departments and food-access nonprofits. Anonymized gap data licensed to distributors.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: USDA admits it has no baseline data on how many stores fail, and its roughly $77M first-year cost estimate describes 'reviewing notice, guidance, and updating stock', which works out to a few hundred dollars per store. That looks far too low against stocking 28 varieties with perishables in tiny coolers, and commenters said so directly: 'refrigerated space is limited for perishable products... would lead to waste and higher operating costs' and 'stocking seven distinct grain varieties... is not feasible for small convenience stores'. Convenience stores are 44% of SNAP retailers but only 5% of redemptions and 76% of sanctions, so many owners will do the math and drop SNAP unless compliance is cheap and certain. The rule also leaves 'perishable' and 'stocking unit' undefined, which creates an interpretation gap that a shared variety ledger can fill. Evidence: final rule https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/05/08/2026-09137/updated-staple-food-stocking-standards-for-retailers-in-the-supplemental-nutrition-assistance and proposed rule https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/09/25/2025-18624/updated-staple-food-stocking-standards-for-retailers-in-the-supplemental-nutrition-assistance
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one metro with dense small-format stores. Sign one cash-and-carry wholesaler or jobber as the kit supplier. Encode the rule's variety-counting logic into a spreadsheet-based counter and walk 40 stores with a $79 audit, aiming for 15 paid audits and 5 kit orders. Publish a one-page 'what counts as a variety' guide and post it in grocer association WhatsApp and Facebook groups. Pitch the local health department a grant-funded 100-store pilot using the audit results as proof.

ideas.title: Medicaid Hours Wallet for Gig Workers
ideas.one_liner: A phone-based monthly proof-of-work ledger that turns gig, cash and self-employment activity into state-accepted documentation and 30-day cure packets, paid for by the Medicaid plans and health centers that lose revenue when members drop.
ideas.customer: Medicaid managed care organizations with expansion-adult lines, and FQHC and community health center networks. Medicaid is 43-50% of health center revenue, and an MCO is paid capitation per member-month. End users are expansion adults aged 19-64 with irregular income. The MCO or health center pays per retained member; the enrollee pays nothing.
ideas.problem: CMS's interim final rule (June 3, 2026) requires states to implement 80 hours a month of work or activity, or $580 a month in income, by Jan 1, 2027. Compliance is checked at application and at renewal, and a noncompliance notice gives 30 calendar days to cure. CBO projects about 4.8M coverage losses from work requirements, largely from reporting complexity. About 9 in 10 affected patients are expected to qualify for an exemption or already comply, yet many will still lose coverage on documentation. Nebraska went live May 1, 2026 with self-attestation, but about 28,000 people there must document twice a year and the state plans to move to verification.
ideas.solution: An enrollee-side SMS and app tool. It ingests bank and payment-app statements, gig platform earnings exports (Uber, DoorDash, Cash App, Venmo), pay stub photos and logged volunteer or class hours. It computes whether each month clears $580 or 80 hours and generates the state-specific verification packet. It sends look-back-month reminders and prepares the 30-day cure response. It flags likely exemption candidates, such as medically frail members, from plan claims data. The plan or clinic dashboard shows at-risk members and cure success. The tool only assists and never determines compliance, which is what federal rules allow plans to do.
ideas.why_now: The interim final rule was published June 3, 2026, and the national start date is Jan 1, 2027. Nebraska's live rollout is the preview of what other states will face when verification replaces self-attestation. CMS is encouraging automation, but states are spending on caseworker portals, notices and screening tools, not on income documentation for gig workers.
ideas.revenue_model: $3-8 per at-risk member per month billed to the MCO, or a success fee of $50-150 per member retained through renewal. FQHC SaaS at $2-5k per month per site with an outcomes dashboard. Later, state contracts for a self-employed and gig documentation module.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Vendors such as Salesforce are building state-facing portals for applicants and caseworkers. The parties with a P&L at stake, the MCOs and health centers, are not yet being sold a member-side tool. KFF's roundup of state outreach plans covers notices, websites and screening tools but does not describe how self-employed or irregular income will be documented (https://www.kff.org/medicaid/medicaid-work-requirements-federal-outreach-requirements-and-state-plans/). State wage-data matching misses 1099, cash and gig work by design. Georgetown's CCF warns that 'verification in this context means burdensome documentation requirements for enrollees' (https://ccf.georgetown.edu/2026/05/11/the-new-medicaid-work-reporting-requirements-are-here-dont-let-the-nebraska-soft-start-fool-you/). The retention math is lopsided: a plan or clinic can pay a few dollars a month per member to protect several hundred dollars of monthly revenue. Sources: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/06/03/2026-11094/medicaid-program-community-engagement-requirement-for-certain-individuals and https://www.pointcare.com/blog/how-to-prevent-medicaid-coverage-gaps-in-2026
ideas.first_30_days: Build the Nebraska flow first, since it is already live. Recruit 50 gig and self-employed Medicaid enrollees through one FQHC partner. Measure how many can produce a compliant $580 or 80-hour packet within 30 days. Take those results to two MCO member-engagement and quality leads for a paid pilot. Sign an LOI with one health center network before Jan 1, 2027.

ideas.title: Cooler-Door Pivot for THC Beverage Brands
ideas.one_liner: A 45-day pivot studio that moves hemp-THC drink and gummy brands into compliant functional products under their existing distributor and retailer slots, plus a per-container THC ledger for distributors and retailers.
ideas.customer: Small and mid-size hemp-THC beverage and edible brands, beverage distributors including alcohol-licensed ones, and convenience, liquor and smoke-shop chains holding hemp SKUs. Brands pay for the pivot sprint and co-pack. Distributors and retailers pay a subscription for the SKU ledger.
ideas.problem: P.L. 119-37 redefines hemp to 0.4 mg total THC per container. The effective date was pushed from Nov 12 to Dec 11, 2026 by H.R. 6500 (signed Sept 2), while synthetic cannabinoids lose hemp status on Nov 12. The US Hemp Roundtable estimates about 95% of existing products fall outside the new definition, and a typical THC drink has 2-10 mg per can. There is no federal sell-through safe harbor. The industry employs about 350,000 people. Distributors are asking whether alcohol-licensed wholesalers can even accept returns in three-tier states, and operators face a liquidity problem, not a compliance problem.
ideas.solution: Two parts. First, an SKU ledger where COAs and pack volumes are converted into per-container total THC (delta-9 plus decarboxylated THCA) and a keep, pull or return status by state, with vendor chargeback letters and a documented disposition trail. Second, a pivot studio that reuses the brand's flavor systems, cans and design to launch adaptogen, functional or non-alcoholic SKUs through a vetted co-packer, so the brand keeps its distributor agreements and planogram slots. An optional bridge licenses the brand to a state-licensed cannabis producer, since licensed dispensaries are unaffected by the federal redefinition.
ideas.why_now: The reprieve to Dec 11 gives roughly 10 weeks. Four congressional frameworks are pending: Barr, Van Duyne and Landsman, Comer, and a Sheehy-Klobuchar Senate companion. The ledger works whether Congress bans or regulates, because age-21, testing and labeling regimes would still need lab-verified per-container data. Retailers and distributors are already telling counsel to audit inventory and plan wind-downs, and gummy prices are reported at 30-50% of 2025 levels.
ideas.revenue_model: $5-15k fixed fee per brand pivot sprint, plus a 2-5% royalty or co-pack margin on the pivot SKUs. $199-499 per month per distributor or retail chain for the SKU ledger and chargeback tooling. Finder fee on brand-licensing deals to licensed operators.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: As Harris Sliwoski puts it, 'The problem for many operators will not be compliance but liquidity' (https://harris-sliwoski.com/cannalawblog/what-the-2026-federal-hemp-ban-means-for-unsold-hemp-inventory/). The scarce asset of a THC-drink brand is not inventory, which is illiquid and repricing downward, but its cooler-door slots and distributor agreements, which are among the hardest things to win in beverages. Those slots vanish if the brand disappears. The per-container standard turns an impossible reformulation into a category switch: LearnBrands notes the demand is being inherited by non-alcoholic beer, alcohol-removed wine and functional beverages (https://www.learnbrands.com/post/hemp-thc-beverage-ban-november-2026). Sources on the reprieve and stakes: https://foleyhoag.com/news-and-insights/blogs/cannabis-and-the-law/2026/september/a-temporary-reprieve-for-hemp-thc-products%E2%80%A6-but-what-now/ and https://www.ediblerank.com/legal/hemp-ban-timeline
ideas.first_30_days: Pull 40 THC-beverage brands from distributor and retailer press lists and offer a free exposure scan built from their COAs and volumes. Sell three paid pivot sprints. Line up one co-packer with non-alcoholic and adaptogen capability. Pilot the SKU ledger with two distributors and one c-store chain, producing their pull and return list.

ideas.title: 1098-VLI Reporting for Small Auto Lenders
ideas.one_liner: Turn a loan tape into IRS-ready Form 1098-VLI statements, with VIN validation and U.S.-final-assembly flags, for credit unions, community banks and buy-here-pay-here dealers that cannot wait for their core vendor.
ideas.customer: Credit unions, community banks, CDFIs, independent auto finance companies, buy-here-pay-here dealers and their loan servicers. Any trade or business receiving $600 or more in interest on a qualifying vehicle loan must report, and the statute has no small-lender exemption. The lender pays per form and per VIN cleanse.
ideas.problem: Treasury's final regulations under IRC 6050AA (published Sept 8, 2026; effective Nov 9, 2026) require Form 1098-VLI showing borrower TIN, interest received, opening principal, origination date and the vehicle's year, make, model and VIN. Statements are due to borrowers by Jan 31 and to the IRS by Feb 28 (Mar 31 if e-filed), with penalties under 6721 and 6722. Transition relief covered 2025, so the 2026 tax year is the first full-form season. The preamble concedes lenders 'may need to collect additional information' and 'may experience difficulties accurately reporting the VIN'. Treasury declined to make lenders verify U.S. assembly, allowing reliance on the VIN plant code or the manufacturer's final-assembly label.
ideas.solution: The lender uploads a CSV from its core or loan origination system. The service validates VIN check digits, decodes them through NHTSA's free decoder, and maps plant-of-manufacture codes through a curated plant-to-final-assembly table it maintains. It screens for new versus used, personal use and origination date, and checks TIN completeness. It produces an exception queue (missing or wrong VINs) with borrower outreach templates. It then generates and delivers the 1098-VLI statements and e-files with the IRS. A white-label web widget for lender sites answers 'is my loan deduction-eligible?'
ideas.why_now: The regs were finalized Sept 8, 2026 and take effect Nov 9. Statements are due Jan 31, 2027, giving four months. Big core processors will serve their largest clients first, and 2026 is the first year without a simple summary-statement safe harbor. The consumer deduction (up to $10,000 of interest on new, U.S.-assembled vehicles under the 2025 tax law) means borrowers will call their lenders asking whether their car qualifies.
ideas.revenue_model: $2-4 per form with a $1,500 annual minimum. $0.25 per loan for VIN cleansing and exception handling. Enterprise license for servicers and core-vendor partners. Consumer eligibility widget with lead-gen to tax preparers or refinance offers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Treasury turned a bright-line rule into a data-quality problem and pushed the risk to the lender. Whether a car is American-assembled is answered by plant-code tables and labels, not by anything in a lender's servicing system, and the preamble openly warns of VIN reporting difficulties. The moat is a curated plant-to-final-assembly table plus an exceptions workflow, which the big vendors will treat as an edge case for small clients. Source: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/09/08/2026-18219/car-loan-interest-deduction (final regs on 6050AA reporting, Form 1098-VLI, the $600 threshold, no small-lender exemption, and the VIN and plant-of-manufacture provisions).
ideas.first_30_days: Build the VIN pipeline on NHTSA's free decoder and validate it on 1,000 real VINs. Offer 30 credit unions a free VIN readiness audit on a 500-loan sample tape and show them their error rate. Publish a plant-code explainer for CU and community bank newsletters. Sign three design partners through state credit union leagues and CUSOs, with a goal of $10k in prepaid annual minimums by December.

ideas.title: Placement Proof for Workforce Pell Providers
ideas.one_liner: A verified job-placement and completion ledger that makes short-term training programs (CDL, CNA, welding, HVAC, medical assistant, cosmetology) audit-ready for the governor and Secretary approvals that Workforce Pell requires.
ideas.customer: Small proprietary career schools, community college workforce and continuing-education units, and employer-training nonprofits running 8-15 week programs. The program owner or director pays. State workforce boards are a second buyer because they were given no new resources to verify placement.
ideas.problem: The Workforce Pell final rule (published May 19, 2026; effective July 20, 2026, with early implementation from July 1) covers programs of 150-599 clock hours and 8-15 weeks. A program must show 70% completion and 70% job placement, measured over the 12 months before it applies and annually after that. The governor must first certify the program as high-skill, high-wage or in-demand, then the Secretary approves. Providers must submit completer lists and the information needed to verify placement. Commenters flagged burden for small providers and noted states got no new resources to run the framework. Separately, the earnings-premium rule (effective July 1, 2027) strips Direct Loan access from programs that fail in two of three consecutive years. The Department estimated 93% of cosmetology programs would fail under the proposal.
ideas.solution: At completion the system automatically sends completers and employers text and email verification requests at 30, 90 and 180 days. It collects pay stubs, employer confirmations and consent for state wage-record matching, and reconciles them to the rule's placement definition. It produces the governor's application packet (completer list, placement evidence, tuition versus earnings benchmarks) and the annual recertification. It also scores each existing program's exposure to the earnings-premium test using public program-level earnings data so owners can decide what to keep, fix or convert into a short-term program.
ideas.why_now: The 12-month look-back means a provider that is not tracking verified placement now cannot apply in 2027. The earnings-premium test takes effect July 1, 2027 and is already being scored on 2021 completers' 2025 earnings. States are building governor-approval processes this fall, and Workforce Pell went live July 2026.
ideas.revenue_model: $4-12k per year per program subscription, or $150-300 per completer verified. $3-5k fixed fee for the governor application packet. Earnings-premium exposure report for $1.5-3k. Later, licensing to state workforce boards for verification.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The binding constraint is not program design but evidence: 70% verified placement with a 12-month clock that starts before the application. Short-course providers such as CDL, CNA and barbering schools typically track completion, not verified employment, so most will discover the gap after the clock has started. The final rule requires providers to give the Governor 'necessary information to verify the job placement rate', and it aggregates small programs' completers up to four award years to reach a 30-student minimum, which favors providers with clean historical records. The Title IV survival angle (93% of cosmetology programs were projected to fail the earnings test under the proposal) gives the same customer a second, more urgent reason to buy. Sources: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/05/19/2026-10013/accountability-in-higher-education-and-access-through-demand-driven-workforce-pell-pell-grant and https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/07/01/2026-13286/accountability-in-higher-education-and-access-through-demand--driven-workforce-pell-student-tuition
ideas.first_30_days: Pick two states whose governors have opened a Workforce Pell approval process. Recruit five schools in different fields, including one at-risk cosmetology school, with a $1.5k pilot price. Backfill the last 12 months of completers by text and employer email to produce a baseline verified placement rate. Deliver a sample governor packet and an earnings-premium exposure score for each. Use the results to pitch the state workforce board on verification capacity.

ideas.title: Exit Ramps for Dying AI Platforms
ideas.one_liner: A converter plus fixed-price migration service that turns Flowise flows, OpenAI Agent Builder graphs and Assistants API integrations into portable, regression-tested code.
ideas.customer: AI automation agencies that have 5-50 client agents built on Flowise, Agent Builder or the Assistants API, and in-house AI teams at SMEs that have no engineer to spare. They pay per migrated agent.
ideas.problem: Three AI platforms are being killed within about 90 days. The Assistants API shut down on 26 Aug 2026. Agent Builder shuts down on 30 Nov 2026. Flowise was archived in mid-Aug 2026 and its core team leaves on 31 Aug. Non-technical teams built visual flows they cannot maintain as raw code. A Flowise insider says forkers 'own dependency updates, security patches, and model API churn indefinitely, and the contributor community that used to absorb that work is dispersing.' A commenter says telling non-engineers to maintain a TypeScript codebase 'is not a real answer.'
ideas.solution: Build importers for Flowise chatflow JSON, Agent Builder workflow exports and Assistants objects (assistants, threads, vector stores, files). They feed a neutral intermediate representation. Exporters then emit (a) Agents SDK / Responses API code, (b) n8n workflows, (c) Langflow. The differentiator is a parity proof. Historical conversation logs are replayed against old and new stacks, and the agency receives a behavioral-diff report it can send to its client. The output is plain, readable code that a coding agent such as Claude Code can maintain. Flowise itself says developers are moving to coding agents because 'rigid workflow low code approach quickly hits the limit.'
ideas.why_now: The Assistants API shutdown (26 Aug 2026), the Agent Builder deadline (30 Nov 2026) and the Flowise archive (Aug 2026) all land in one quarter, which forces spending on a real deadline. Coding agents now make code-first output maintainable by non-experts. Flowise has 55.5k stars and 25k forks, so the stranded installed base is large.
ideas.revenue_model: Fixed-price migration of $500-2,500 per agent. An agency plan of $199/mo keeps flows mirrored in the intermediate representation with a nightly 'can I still leave?' test. The free converter CLI is the lead magnet.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The demand is a deadline plus a maintenance gap, not a tooling gap. Evidence: OpenAI's deprecations page gives the Agent Builder shutdown as 30 Nov 2026 and the Assistants API as 26 Aug 2026 (https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/deprecations). Flowise's sunset notice sets the code freeze, the archive and the end of core-team support (https://flowiseai.com/sunset). The GitHub repo shows 55.5k stars, 25k forks and 699 open issues (https://github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise). The HN thread quotes the 'not a real answer' complaint and notes that OpenAI's own Agent Builder is also going away (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49176920). Agencies that resell agents to clients are the buyers, and they carry portfolio risk that a single hobbyist does not. The parity report is what they sell on to their clients.
ideas.first_30_days: Week 1: mine the Flowise Discord, GitHub issues and r/n8n for stranded users. Ship a free 'flowise-to-n8n / Agents SDK' CLI that handles the 3 most common node types. Weeks 2-3: cold-DM 40 agencies and sell 5-10 pilot migrations at $750, prioritizing Agent Builder users before the 30 Nov deadline. Week 4: turn the manual steps in those migrations into automated exporters and publish before/after parity reports as case studies.

ideas.title: TurkBridge: MTurk-Compatible Verified-Human Marketplace
ideas.one_liner: An MTurk requester-API-compatible endpoint backed by an identity-verified, proof-of-human worker pool, launched as Amazon Mechanical Turk closes on 30 Sept 2026.
ideas.customer: Academic labs and survey researchers, small ML data-labeling teams, and apps that use human-in-the-loop micro-tasks through boto3 or psiTurk-style code. Displaced MTurk workers are the supply side.
ideas.problem: Amazon closes MTurk on 30 Sept 2026 and the FAQ names no alternatives or migration path. New HITs end 30 Sept, bonuses are possible until 30 Oct, and transaction history is inaccessible after 28 Jan 2027. SageMaker Ground Truth and Augmented AI lose the MTurk worker type on the same date. Requesters have legacy code and no drop-in replacement, and quality was already collapsing because workers submitted AI output. One HN user says their app 'has been using Amazon Mechanical Turk for left-pad queries, and that service is shutting down in less than two weeks.'
ideas.solution: (1) Publish an API shim that mimics the MTurk requester operations (CreateHIT, ListAssignmentsForHIT, ApproveAssignment, qualification requirements, sandbox), so a codebase migrates by changing an endpoint URL. (2) Build supply from ex-MTurk workers on Turkopticon and worker forums, who lose income on the closure date. Give each worker a verified unique-person identity, passkey and liveness checks, and behavioural anti-LLM signals. (3) Sell two tiers, 'verified human' and 'domain expert', with paid-per-task quality gates. The product is the proof that a human did the work, priced above the old race-to-the-bottom rate.
ideas.why_now: The shutdown date is two days away, and worker income disappears the same day. Generic open crowd platforms have been wrecked by LLMs, so verified humanness has become the scarce good. Identity-verification APIs are now cheap (Didit, 'Stripe for Identity Verification', launched on HN in March 2026).
ideas.revenue_model: A 20-30% take on task payments, a $99/mo lab plan with participant-screening tools, and a per-verification fee for enterprise annotation buyers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is trust in who is doing the task, and the API compatibility is what lets you take the customers. The MTurk FAQ confirms the dates and lists no alternative or migration path (https://www.mturk.com/help). In the 534-point HN thread (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49457545), dubeye writes: 'The problem as I see it is verifying the work is not done by AI. If it was possible to verify somehow that the work is definitely not done by AI I think there would still be a market.' Another user found MNIST accuracy from Ground Truth on MTurk 'marginally better than guessing.' Prolific is named as the maintained alternative, but I found no evidence that any alternative offers MTurk API compatibility. Legacy scripts are the switching cost, and the shim removes it.
ideas.first_30_days: Week 1: write the shim covering the 6 most-used MTurk operations, using boto3's endpoint_url override. Post a 'migrate in 10 minutes' guide on r/mturk, psiTurk and academic Twitter. Weeks 2-3: onboard the first 300-500 workers with ID and liveness checks. Recruit 5 lab requesters with free credits in exchange for case studies. Week 4: run paid studies, publish a proof-of-human quality comparison against raw MTurk data, and start charging the take rate.

ideas.title: Data Estate Broker for Main Street Closures
ideas.one_liner: An appraisal-and-brokerage service that finds, de-identifies and sells the operational exhaust (quotes, work orders, dispatch logs, inspection records) of retiring or closing non-tech firms to AI buyers.
ideas.customer: Owners, business brokers, insolvency practitioners and CPAs handling closures of small manufacturers, freight brokers, insurance agencies, energy contractors and engineering firms. The buyers are vertical-AI startups and labs that need real workflow data.
ideas.problem: Failed-company data is now valuable. Google bought bankrupt Spirit Airlines' data for $10M: 100M emails, 30M+ recorded calls, 763,000+ flights of ops data, 1.2M fuel slips and 787,452 parts purchases. Mercor was the underbidder. But SimpleClosure, the main shutdown broker, only serves VC-backed startups, whose H1 2026 shutdowns were 27.3% B2B SaaS and 14.4% AI. Buyers say they want scarce data from manufacturing, energy, banking, insurance, professional services and logistics. Those firms close or retire constantly and have nobody to appraise or sell their data.
ideas.solution: Start with operational, non-consumer-PII data, which is the least legally fraught. Examples are work orders, quotes and bids, dispatch and routing logs, inspection and maintenance records, CAD revision histories, and internal Q&A threads. Run a 'data asset scan' ($500-1,500, credited against fees), then rights review and de-identification. Package the results as licensed corpora, run a sealed-bid sale to vertical-AI buyers and take a 25-35% success fee. Recruit business brokers, liquidators and trade associations as referral partners. Consumer call recordings and customer emails are excluded until counsel signs off.
ideas.why_now: Buyers proved a price in Aug 2026 (Spirit, $10M) and there is a losing bidder waiting. SimpleClosure's own asset report shows buyers paying tens to hundreds of thousands for unique corpora and wanting 'how real work actually got done.' Vertical AI agents for trades and logistics need training data that does not exist on the open web. Small-business retirements are a multi-year wave, and Sherline Tools going out of business (Sept 2026) is one example.
ideas.revenue_model: 25-35% success fee on data licence sales, plus a $500-1,500 appraisal fee credited against it. Optional recurring 'living licence' fees for firms that stay open.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The market for dead-company data exists, but the only broker is aimed at software startups, while buyers explicitly want boring industries. Evidence: Google's $10M Spirit purchase with Mercor as underbidder (https://www.theregister.com/ai-and-ml/2026/08/18/google-buys-crashed-airline-spirits-data-at-auction-because-ai/5288962). The HN discussion notes that Scale, Surge and Mercor are recreating workplace data (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49343559). SimpleClosure's asset report lists 'manufacturing, energy, banking, insurance, professional services, logistics' as scarce-data buyers (https://simpleclosure.com/blog/insights/what-your-assets-are-worth/). Its H1 2026 report shows its funnel is startups (https://simpleclosure.com/blog/insights/state-of-shutdowns-h1-2026/). The main risk is privacy backlash. HN commenters doubt the de-identification ('I'm skeptical it'll be wiped correctly'), so the wedge is operational data with no consumer PII.
ideas.first_30_days: Week 1: pick two verticals, for example machine shops and freight brokerage. Book 20 calls with business brokers and CPAs who handle closures. Weeks 2-3: sign 3 exclusive listing agreements on a free data-asset scan. Line up 5 buyer LOIs from vertical-AI startups building quoting or dispatch agents. Week 4: complete one appraisal, get a privacy-counsel template for rights review, and run the first sealed-bid process.

ideas.title: Cloud-Bricking Escrow for Hardware Brands
ideas.one_liner: A neutral escrow-and-standby service that holds a hardware brand's cloud backend and local-mode firmware, and takes over the moment the cloud vendor fails.
ideas.customer: Consumer-hardware brands that outsource their cloud or app to an ODM or startup: private-label and licensed smart-home, router, EV-charger, pet-tech and e-bike brands. Retailers and insurers are secondary buyers.
ideas.problem: When a small backend vendor dies, the brand that sold the device takes the blame. Motorola-branded routers stopped being manageable when the MotoSync+ app failed. Play Store reviews say a third-party backend host's licence expired and the host ended operations ('Server Licence Expired'). Users report months without a fix. Spotify Car Thing became 'a $200 hardware turned into e-waste overnight.' An HN commenter estimated $300k-600k to open-source a single project, so afterthought rescue is unaffordable.
ideas.solution: For a flat annual fee, the brand deposits its backend container images and infrastructure-as-code, sealed secrets, signed 'local mode' firmware or companion-app builds, and device protocol docs. The operator monitors cloud health, domain and cert expiry, app-store status and vendor solvency signals. On a trigger it either runs the backend on standby infrastructure (pay-per-device) or releases the local-mode build. Brands that certify get an 'Afterlife Ready' mark for retail listings and regulator conversations.
ideas.why_now: EU Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations began on 11 Sept 2026, with full manufacturer obligations from 11 Dec 2027 and lifecycle handling required. Startup shutdowns are running at a high rate: 14.4% of H1 2026 shutdowns were AI companies with a median age of 2.3 years and a median $30k cash at closure. Recent bricking cases (Motorola routers in Jun 2026, Nest thermostats, Kodak Pulse frames, Samsung fridges in Sept 2026) are fresh in retailers' minds.
ideas.revenue_model: $5-25k/yr escrow subscription per brand, plus $0.10-0.50/device/month for hot standby and a per-incident recovery fee. Certification audits are a later add-on.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The liability chain runs from a dead vendor through the brand to the customer, and existing escrow (software licence escrow, to my knowledge) is not built for live device fleets. Evidence: the Motorola router thread (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48425611, 238 points) traces the outage to a third-party server licence expiring after the host company ended operations. The 'when hardware goes EOL' essay (https://www.marcia.no/words/eol; HN discussion at https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46609492, 403 points) lists Nest, Car Thing and Kodak Pulse. It quotes the $300k-600k open-sourcing estimate and community workarounds (OpenWRT, 'No Longer Evil'). The EU CRA page (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cyber-resilience-act) sets the 11 Sept 2026 and 11 Dec 2027 dates. The buyer is the brand, not the consumer, and the fee has to be cheaper than a single recall.
ideas.first_30_days: Week 1: build a free 'BackendWatch' monitor that pings a brand's cloud endpoints, cert expiry and domain renewals. Week 2: cold-email 50 licensed-brand and private-label hardware companies, and Kickstarter-scale hardware founders. Weeks 3-4: sign 3 design partners on a $2.5k pilot escrow. Write the trigger contract with a startup-insolvency lawyer.

ideas.title: Sunset Software Co: Pledge-Funded Tool Revival
ideas.one_liner: When a B2B tool announces its shutdown, customers pre-commit to paid 'extended life' contracts, and a small operator takes over only if a threshold is met.
ideas.customer: Companies stranded when a small dev or data tool shuts down or is acqui-hired away: CI runners, SQL clients, project trackers, metrics services. The founder of the dying tool is the second counterparty and receives a revenue share.
ideas.problem: Acqui-hires and product-gap closures strand paying customers with 30-90 days notice. BuildJet closed runners on 31 Mar 2026 because 'GitHub has made substantial improvements.' Cirrus CI closed on 1 Jun 2026 when Cirrus Labs joined OpenAI. Garnix shut down after being acquired. One customer wrote 'I have two CI providers to replace by the end of the Quarter.' Founders cannot sell the code. An Ask HN founder 'couldn't sell the codebase', and a commenter said 'no one wants some abandoned open source project for a defunct business.' PopSQL, SeekWell and Pivotal Tracker left solo builders racing to fill the gap.
ideas.solution: Run a 'continuity pledge' during the notice window. The customer signs a 12-month extended-life contract at 1.2-1.5x the old price, conditional on the operator reaching a minimum pledge total, like a Kickstarter for revival. If the threshold is met, the operator takes a code and brand licence, keeps the service running with a founder retainer or revenue share, and gets paid from day one. If not, nobody pays and nothing is bought. Portfolio economics do the rest: many small tools, shared infrastructure, no CAC.
ideas.why_now: AI-lab and platform acqui-hires now regularly turn small devtools into shutdown notices. Cirrus Labs joined OpenAI, Bun joined Anthropic, Astro joined Cloudflare, and Tailwind joined Shopify in the last year. The acquirer wants the team, not the customers. Permissive licences (Cirrus relicensed Tart and related tools as 'more permissive') make forks legal. The SimpleClosure H1 2026 report shows shutdowns running at scale.
ideas.revenue_model: 60-80% of extended-life fees kept by the operator, with 20-40% shared with the founder for 12 months. Later, cross-sell hosted plans to the open-source user base.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: A dying tool's code has no buyers, but its running service has customers who will pay. The sellable asset is customer continuity, and the pledge threshold removes the risk of buying dead code. Evidence: the Ask HN thread has a founder who could not sell his codebase and a commenter saying no one wants an abandoned project (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44398065). Cirrus CI's closure and Tart relicensing are covered at https://cirruslabs.org/ (HN discussion 47730194, 282 points). The Garnix thread has the 'two CI providers to replace by the end of the Quarter' comment (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48317043). BuildJet's notice sets the 31 Mar 2026 date (https://buildjet.com/for-github-actions/blog/we-are-shutting-down). Demand for a replacement shows up as solo builders rushing in, for example Saturn SQL after PopSQL and SeekWell (https://saturnsql.com) and the 10 teams racing to replace Pivotal Tracker (https://bye-tracker.net).
ideas.first_30_days: Week 1: set up a monitor on HN, status pages and changelogs for shutdown announcements. Week 2: pick one tool currently in its notice window and email the founder with a 12-month revenue-share offer. Weeks 3-4: publish a pledge page for that tool with a fixed pledge threshold and a 21-day deadline. If it clears the threshold, sign the licence and run the tool on shared infrastructure.

ideas.title: Buy the Orphaned License of Dead Models
ideas.one_liner: Acquire or secure exclusive commercial-licensing rights to hugely downloaded open models and tools whose company died, then sell clean, warranted commercial licenses plus a public orphan-license registry.
ideas.customer: Startups and mid-size companies shipping voice features (dubbing, audiobooks, IVR, game NPC voices, accessibility) on top of XTTS-class models, and the procurement or legal teams of their enterprise buyers who now ask for model-license provenance.
ideas.problem: Coqui XTTS-v2 is still pulled about 6.75M times a month under a non-commercial license (CPML), but Coqui shut down in Dec 2023. Commercial licensing was 'available upon inquiry' from a company that no longer exists, so builders either violate the license, ship legal risk to customers, or rip out the best multilingual voice-cloning model. GitHub threads asking about commercial use or the license after shutdown were closed 'wontfix'.
ideas.solution: Phase 1: trace the rights chain (Coqui Inc., founders, assignees, any bankruptcy or dissolution filings) and option an exclusive commercial-licensing agency deal or outright IP purchase, which should be cheap because the seller is a dead startup. Phase 2: sell per-product annual commercial licenses ($2k-$25k) with a written rights-chain warranty and an audit letter that customers can hand to enterprise procurement. Phase 3: publish an Orphan Model Registry (model, steward status, license, who can grant commercial rights) as a free lead-gen asset and a paid API for AI-governance tools. Fallback if the rights-holder refuses: sell a fixed-price license-risk audit and a swap-to-permissive-model migration (Apache/MIT TTS) with regression tests.
ideas.why_now: Enterprise AI-governance questionnaires in 2026 ask for model and data provenance. The $1.5B Anthropic authors settlement (2025) and the Authors Guild v. OpenAI/Microsoft unsealed briefs (HN front page 2026-09-27, 626 points) made license hygiene a board-level topic.
