Open voice tools are exploding: VoiceStudio hit 43.9k stars, +27k in one month, and its README warns each bundled model has its own license to review before commercial use.
ideas.revenue_model: Annual per-product licenses ($2k-$25k), enterprise-wide licenses, audit and migration fees ($3k-$8k fixed price), registry API subscription ($200-$1k a month).
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Demand is already proven and supply is literally zero: nobody can sell a commercial license because the seller is dead, so dead-startup IP is the scarcest cheap asset in open AI. Evidence: XTTS-v2 shows 6,752,613 downloads last month under CPML (https://huggingface.co/coqui/XTTS-v2). Coqui repo issues on commercial use, license after shutdown and 'Move to MIT' are closed wontfix (https://github.com/coqui-ai/TTS/issues?q=commercial+license+is%3Aissue). Issue #4022, opened nearly a year after shutdown, says the community is confused about 'commercial use and fine-tuning' (https://github.com/coqui-ai/TTS/issues/4022). HN, Nov 2023: XTTS stays non-commercial with commercial licensing 'upon inquiry'. VoiceStudio's AGPL repo warns model licenses vary (https://github.com/debpalash/VoiceStudio).
ideas.first_30_days: Days 1-7: pull Delaware and other corporate records for Coqui Inc., message the founders and former staff, and draft a one-page option agreement (small cash plus revenue share). Days 1-10: build the registry from 50 popular non-commercial or orphaned models on Hugging Face. Days 10-30: email companies that opened XTTS licensing issues and companies whose products visibly use XTTS (from public GitHub dependency graphs) with a $3k risk audit, and aim for 3-5 paid audits. If the rights option lands, convert those audits into licenses.

ideas.title: H.264 Royalty Sunset Desk for Streamers
ideas.one_liner: A country-by-country patent-expiry analysis and codec-delivery plan that cuts H.264/AVC streaming royalty exposure for mid-tier video services, paid partly on savings.
ideas.customer: Mid-size OTT and FAST channel operators, ed-tech, fitness, telehealth and cloud-gaming platforms and video-heavy social apps (well below the 100M-subscriber mega-tier). Buyer is the general counsel, CFO or head of video engineering.
ideas.problem: The Via LA AVC pool replaced its flat $100k streaming cap with tiered fees up to $4.5M a year, and added FAST and cloud-gaming categories, for a codec standardized in 2003. Press reports say US patent coverage runs out around 2028, so one analysis says paying $4.5M for about 18 months of coverage 'makes no economic sense'. Wikipedia and HN commenters put at least one US patent at 2030 and 'only 5 left' worldwide. Mid-tier operators can't tell what they actually owe.
ideas.solution: Ingest Via LA's public AVC patent attachment (re-issued 2026-09-28) plus national legal-status data, and build a live-patent map per country. Overlay each customer's audience by country and device. Deliver (a) a counsel-ready exposure memo to negotiate the right tier or challenge scope, (b) an engineering plan that serves AV1/VP9 in territories with live patents and H.264 where none remain, using a device-capability ladder, and (c) a countdown dashboard that also tracks HEVC and audio codecs. Work with a patent attorney partner so the memo is legal work product.
ideas.why_now: The new streaming fee schedule took effect in early 2026 (Tom's Hardware, Apr 3, 2026: fees raised 'from $100,000 up to $4.5 million'). The last MPEG-4 Part 2 patent expired 2026-07-19 and the last E-AC3 patents may have lapsed in 2026, so 'is it free yet?' is a live question. AV1 hardware decode is now common in 2023+ phones, TVs and PCs.
ideas.revenue_model: Fixed $15k-$40k audit and plan, plus about 20% of first-year royalty savings or avoided fees, plus $1k a month for the monitoring dashboard.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Patent pools price by audience tier, not by how many patents are still alive, and patents are territorial and expire on different dates, so the expiry calendar itself is arbitrage. Evidence: Via LA's program page shows Tier 1 at $4.5M a year, small operators as low as $100k, new FAST and cloud-gaming tiers, and a patent attachment updated 2026-09-28 (https://www.via-la.com/licensing-2/avc-h-264/). The Wikipedia AVC entry notes many patents expired but at least one US patent runs to Nov 2030, and that Nokia sued HP and Amazon over H.264/H.265 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Video_Coding). The HN thread on the last Brazilian MPEG-4 patent expiring includes 'only 5 left' and a Siemens patent to 2030 (https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/items/49311814). Details of the expired Siemens BR patent: https://www.xda-developers.com/25-year-old-brazilian-video-patent-expired-legal-headache-linux/.
ideas.first_30_days: Days 1-14: scrape the Via LA patent list and build the per-country expiry table for AVC (a few weekends of work). Days 10-30: post the free 'H.264 patent death clock' as a public page, pitch 30 mid-size streaming and video-first SaaS companies from job boards and app-store data with a free exposure estimate, and offer a $7.5k pilot audit to the first 3 who reply. Retain a patent attorney on a flat fee to sign off on memo templates.

ideas.title: Rights-Cleared 1929-1963 Corpus for AI
ideas.one_liner: Join scanned mid-century books, magazines and newspapers to Copyright Office renewal records to produce provably public-domain text for AI training, with libraries paid a share and spared the scraper load.
ideas.customer: AI labs, foundation-model startups and fine-tuning shops that need litigation-proof training data, plus library and archive partners who supply scans (buyer is head of data or general counsel).
ideas.problem: Clean training data is now a legal necessity, but the best public-domain corpus (Harvard's Institutional Books 1.0, 983,004 volumes, 242B tokens) is largely pre-1929 text. For US works published 1929-1963, copyright lapsed unless renewed, yet renewals were rare (a 1961 Copyright Office study found fewer than 15% of registered copyrights renewed). The registration and renewal records exist but nobody has joined them to scanned text at scale. Meanwhile libraries are drowning in AI bots and have no sustainable way to offer their collections.
ideas.solution: Take scans that already exist (Internet Archive, partner libraries, HathiTrust-style holdings). Match each volume to Catalog of Copyright Entries registrations and renewals (Stanford renewal database for 1923-1949 books; Copyright Office online records for 1950+), and exclude foreign works restored under the URAA. Output a per-volume rights dossier with evidence links and a confidence score. Sell dataset snapshots with a signed provenance certificate (and insurance-backed warranty as revenue grows). Offer participating libraries a paid bulk-snapshot mirror (S3 or rsync) so AI buyers stop scraping their sites, with a revenue share.
ideas.why_now: The Authors Guild v. OpenAI/Microsoft unsealed briefs (2026-09-27) claim executives knew mass book piracy was illegal. Harvard and OpenAI/Microsoft-backed public-domain releases show buyers want clean data. Creative Commons (Aug 2026) says heritage institutions need standardized 'prosocial conditions' for AI access, and some (the National Library of the Netherlands, Trove) have closed access.
ideas.revenue_model: Dataset licenses ($25k-$250k per slice or annual refresh), provenance certificate fees, revenue share paid to libraries, bespoke rights-clearance projects for publishers reissuing out-of-print titles.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck for legal AI text isn't scanning, it's rights determination: a huge band of 1929-1963 US works is public domain because nobody filed a renewal, and it's invisible until someone does the record join at scale. Libraries currently do this by hand. Evidence: Institutional Books 1.0 covers 983,004 volumes and 242B tokens (https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08300). Wikipedia notes non-renewed pre-1964 works are public domain, the 1961 study, and the databases that hold the records (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright_renewal). GLAM-E Lab survey: 39 of 43 institutions (91%) saw traffic surges, 69% of those blamed AI training bots, 74% deployed countermeasures, and robots.txt was largely ignored (https://glamelab.org/products/are-ai-bots-knocking-cultural-heritage-offline/). Creative Commons Aug 2026 on institutions closing access (https://creativecommons.org/2026/08/19/open-heritage-in-the-age-of-artificial-intelligence/). Authors Guild briefs, HN 626 points (https://authorsguild.org/news/ag-v-openai-top-execs-knew-mass-book-piracy-was-illegal/).
ideas.first_30_days: Days 1-10: pick a narrow, high-value slice (for example 1950-1963 US trade, technical and hobby magazines where renewal was nearly nonexistent) and download the matching Internet Archive scans and renewal records. Days 10-25: run a first 5,000-volume join, have a copyright attorney sign off on the method and the URAA exclusions, and publish a free 500-volume sample with dossiers. Days 25-30: send the sample to 15 AI data buyers and licensed-data startups and to 5 mid-size libraries for a mirror pilot. Target one paid pilot in 90 days.

ideas.title: CRA Ten-Year Update Vault for Vendors
ideas.one_liner: An escrow-plus-hosting service that keeps a small vendor's signed security updates, vulnerability intake and orphaned open-source dependencies alive for the EU Cyber Resilience Act's ten-year obligation if the vendor folds or an upstream dies.
ideas.customer: Small EU-selling firmware, IoT and software vendors (1-50 staff) with no security team, and the enterprise buyers and OEMs who will demand proof of continuity before they buy from them.
ideas.problem: CRA reporting duties started 2026-09-11 and the main obligations bite 2027-12-11, with no size exemption. A solo German software founder on HN (Sept 1, 2026) calls the requirement that security updates stay available for ten years, or the support period if longer, a critical burden, and notes reporting duties continue after support ends. Harmonised standards aren't published yet (core standards due Oct 31, 2026). Open-source upstreams also vanish: MinIO (61.3k stars) was archived on 2026-04-25 with no binaries, and 'no fork has gained traction'.
ideas.solution: Three parts. (1) Escrow: a reproducible-build environment, SBOM/VEX and split-custody signing keys held by the vault, released on contractual trigger events (insolvency, abandonment, twelve months without a patch). (2) Continuity hosting: a signed-update endpoint and advisory feed that stays online for ten years, plus a vulnerability-report intake and drafts for the EU single reporting platform. (3) Dependency lifeboat: patch backports and maintained forks of orphaned components that customers depend on (MinIO first). Vendors get a 'continuity certificate' to attach to tenders.
ideas.why_now: Reporting obligations are 17 days old as of today, standards are still being written, and small vendors are asking on HN what to do. The EU's own guidance creates open-source 'stewards' who face obligations but are exempt from fines, while manufacturers carry the burden, so the market will look for a commercial steward.
ideas.revenue_model: Annual escrow and hosting fee per product (EUR 1.5k-6k), a per-release fee, trigger-event activation fee, and dependency-lifeboat support contracts priced per node.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The CRA turns 'what if you disappear?' from a founder worry into a legal duty, and escrow-style insurance sells to both the vendor and the buyer who fears the vendor's death; the compliance-tooling crowd (scanners, SBOM dashboards) does not cover it. Evidence: Ask HN by a one-person vendor on the ten-year update rule, harmonised standards timing and no size exemption (https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/items/49520688). The EU says stewards are not subject to administrative fines (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cra-open-source), with the 11 Sept 2026 and 11 Dec 2027 dates at https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cyber-resilience-act. Linux Foundation research finds most open-source respondents unfamiliar with the CRA and its deadlines (https://linuxfoundation.org/research/cra-readiness). Greg Kroah-Hartman's explainer says the burden lands on commercial manufacturers (https://www.theregister.com/2025/09/30/cyber_reiliance_act_opinion_column/). Upstream death example: https://github.com/minio/minio.
ideas.first_30_days: Days 1-10: write the escrow and trigger-event contract template with an EU tech lawyer, and prototype a reproducible-build capture for one embedded Linux and one Go or Rust project. Days 10-30: post a plain-English 'CRA ten-year problem' guide on HN, the Open Regulatory Compliance working group hub and embedded-vendor communities, and offer 10 founders a free continuity assessment. Sell 3 paid pilot vaults at a founder price of EUR 1k a year. In parallel, publish a MinIO advisory-and-patch feed to test paying demand for the lifeboat.

ideas.title: Lot-Level Verification for Generic Semaglutide Importers
ideas.one_liner: A shared-API lineage database plus independent identity and impurity testing for distributors and pharmacy chains buying the flood of post-patent generic semaglutide.
ideas.customer: Distributors, pharmacy chains, hospital groups and telehealth clinics in India, Canada, Brazil and the 75+ markets Indian exporters like Hetero now target, and payers or regulators who need lot-level evidence.
ideas.problem: Semaglutide patents lapsed in Canada (Jan 2026), India and Brazil (Mar 2026), and 40+ Indian companies launched brands within weeks. By July, Dr. Reddy's halted supply through at least late October over an API impurity, and Torrent recalled Semalix batches after Dr. Reddy's notice because it uses the same API. Buyers can't see which brands share which API source, and fake pens circulate.
ideas.solution: Build an API-lineage graph from customs and shipping records, regulatory notices, recalls and public dossiers, mapping each brand and batch to its API manufacturer, and alert subscribers when any brand in the shared-API cluster has an event. Pair this with fast lot testing (LC-MS peptide identity and purity, impurity profile) through accredited partner labs in India, the UAE and Brazil, returning a signed 'verified lot' certificate with QR lookup. Start with a free public recall-radar page and newsletter to collect buyers.
ideas.why_now: Generics launched in March-July 2026 across three large markets at once (India prices as low as Rs 1,500 a month), regulators are stretched, and the first recalls and counterfeit guidance are already published. Tirzepatide and US semaglutide remain patented, so the gray market will keep growing alongside the legitimate one.
ideas.revenue_model: $250-$600 per verified lot, $500-$2,000 a month for lineage alerts and API access, and custom supplier audits for hospital groups and exporters.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Forty-plus brands is not forty-plus independent risks: a handful of API sources means one impurity event propagates across supposedly competing brands, and no buyer-side tool maps that. Evidence: BusinessLine's headline 'DRL's semaglutide supply hits a stumbling block, affects other companies too' and Economic Times' Torrent recall after Dr. Reddy's notice (Jul 9, 2026) via Google News (https://news.google.com/rss/search?q=Torrent+Semalix+recall+Dr+Reddy%27s+API+semaglutide+Canada); Fierce Pharma on the pause (https://www.fiercepharma.com/manufacturing/dr-reddys-presses-pause-generic-semaglutide-supply-after-flagging-api-issue). India Today: 'Quality concerns hit cheap Ozempic copies in India within months'. NDTV, Mar 30, 2026: 'How To Spot Fakes'. Hetero: 1.5M pens, 75+ markets (Medical Dialogues Apr 16, 2026). Patent-expiry dates and 40-50 brands: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semaglutide.
ideas.first_30_days: Days 1-7: assemble a public database of every Indian semaglutide brand, the marketing-authorization holder, contract manufacturer and any disclosed API source, and ship the recall-radar page. Days 7-20: sign a testing-lab partner in India or the UAE on a wholesale per-lot price, and run 20 lots bought retail as a published 'state of the market' report. Days 20-30: pitch 25 importers, pharmacy chains and telehealth clinics with a free lineage check plus a $400 lot test, and aim for 5 paid tests.
